newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: Mauritius says preferential sugar trade vital.
newsitem.headline: Mauritius says preferential sugar trade vital.

text.p: Mauritius said on Tuesday that its social and economic development would be jeopardised if its mainstay product, sugar, was not able to continue enjoying preferential access to European markets.

Opening the 11th council meeting of the International Sugar Organization in the Indian Ocean island, Prime Minister Navinchandra Ramgoolam urged that his country's sugar exports remain protected in the face of mounting free market pressures.

"The stable earnings from the sugar protocol have allowed the Mauritian government to undertake important development programmes in a wide range of sectors such as health, education, housing, social security and public infrastructure," Ramgoolam told delegates.
"(Without the sugar earnings this) development would have been near impossible or taken much longer to achieve."
Under a 1975 protocol between the European Union and developing African, Caribbean and Pacific (ACP) countries, Mauritius can each year export some 580,000 tonnes of sugar to the markets of Europe.
This quota for the island makes up the bulk of its average annual crop which in 1996 totalled 588,455 tonnes.
Another preferential treaty guarantees the sale of additional raw sugar from Mauritius, where the industry provides jobs for around 35,000 small planters, for refining to the EU.

Arvin Boolell, Mauritius's minister of agriculture and natural resources, said the diversification of the island's economy into sectors including textiles and tourism had flowed from the use of revenue from sugar sales under the protocol.
But the recent Uruguay Round of GATT trade talks, which raised strong doubts about global tariff protection, now threatens the favoured nation status of Mauritius.
"Today the advocates of trade liberalisation are desparately trying to convince us that the world will be a better place to live if there were no tariffs or subsidies..," Boolell said.
